title: Can You Sell AI-Generated Books on Amazon KDP? Rules & Risks
meta_description: Can you sell AI-generated books on Amazon KDP? Yes, if you disclose. See KDP's AI rules, copyright limits, rejection risks and an 8-step checklist.
quick_answer: Yes. Amazon KDP lets you sell books containing AI-generated text, images or translations, but you must disclose that content when you publish or republish the title. If you created the content yourself and used AI only to edit it or brainstorm ideas, that's AI-assisted and needs no disclosure. Books must still meet KDP's content guidelines, and purely AI-made material may not be protected by copyright.
key_takeaways: KDP allows AI-generated content, but you must disclose AI-generated text, images and translations when you publish or republish a title.
AI-assisted work doesn't need disclosing under KDP's current guidance. That means content you created yourself and then edited, error-checked or brainstormed with AI.
Heavy editing doesn't turn AI output into AI-assisted work. KDP still counts it as AI-generated.
In the U.S., text and images made entirely by AI generally can't be copyrighted, so you may not be able to stop copycats.
Disclosure doesn't mean your book passes a quality check. KDP can block or remove low-quality, duplicate or misleading books, and repeated problems can put your account at risk.
Keep an AI log for each book so your disclosure answers are accurate and easy to update. Always re-read KDP's current Content Guidelines before you publish.
who_this_is_for: This guide is for first-time and indie authors who want to use ChatGPT, Claude or an image generator to help make a Kindle eBook or paperback and need to understand KDP's AI rules and risks before they click Publish.
intro: AI tools can draft a manuscript, design a cover and translate a book in an afternoon, so it's natural to ask whether Amazon will let you sell the result. It will, but there are conditions that many first-time authors miss. This guide explains KDP's AI disclosure rule in plain language, shows where the line between AI-generated and AI-assisted content falls, and gives you a simple AI log template for answering KDP's disclosure question accurately. It also covers the copyright, quality and competition risks that decide whether a book made with AI is worth publishing, plus an 8-step checklist for making one that adds real value. There are no income promises here. Results on KDP vary widely and depend on the book.

steps.name: Read KDP's current AI and content rules
steps.text: In KDP Help, open the Content Guidelines page. Read the artificial intelligence section in full, along with the sections on rights, metadata and disappointing content. Menu names change, so if you can't find the AI section, search KDP Help for 'AI-generated content'. Write down the date you checked.

steps.name: Pick a topic where you add something AI can't
steps.text: Choose a subject where you have real expertise, experience, original research or an audience you know well. Search Amazon for the exact phrase a buyer would type and look through the first few pages of results. If they're full of near-identical books, find a sharper angle or choose another topic.

steps.name: Decide AI's role and start an AI log
steps.text: Before you write, decide where AI will help: outlining, drafting, editing, the cover or translation. Start a simple log for the book that records which tool created or edited each part, using the template later in this guide. The log makes KDP's disclosure question easy to answer accurately.

steps.name: Write or rebuild the draft in your own voice
steps.text: Whether you start from a blank page or an AI draft, add what only you can: examples from your own work, stories, case studies, worksheets, and photos and data you gathered yourself. Cut repetition and generic filler. Remember that heavily edited AI text still counts as AI-generated when you disclose.

steps.name: Fact-check every claim and source
steps.text: Check facts, figures, quotes and references against the original sources. Delete any citation you can't find, because AI tools can invent them. Take extra care with health, safety, legal and money topics, and consider asking a qualified expert to review those sections.

steps.name: Edit, format and proof like a professional
steps.text: Have a human editor or trusted beta readers review the structure and clarity. Use Kindle Previewer to check how your eBook looks on different devices. For paperbacks, order a printed proof copy to catch problems with images, margins and resolution.

steps.name: Make your cover and metadata honest
steps.text: Check AI cover art for distorted hands, garbled text and any resemblance to existing covers. Use a title and subtitle that describe the book accurately, without stuffing them with keywords. Never use another author's name, a trademark or a look-alike of a bestseller.

steps.name: Disclose accurately, publish and maintain
steps.text: Answer KDP's AI question truthfully for text, images and translations, using your AI log. If you add AI-generated content later, update your answer when you republish. After launch, read reviews, fix errors and upload revised files. Keep records of royalties and expenses for tax purposes.

sections.heading: Can You Sell AI-Generated Books on Amazon KDP? The Short Answer
paragraphs: Yes. Amazon KDP lets you publish and sell books that contain AI-generated content, as long as you disclose that content when you set up the title and the book meets the same content guidelines as every other KDP book.

Amazon added an AI disclosure requirement to the KDP content guidelines in 2023. When you publish a new title, or edit and republish an existing one, KDP asks whether you used AI-based tools to create the book's text, images or translations. Your answer must be accurate.

Disclosing AI use is about transparency, not approval. A book with full AI disclosure can still be blocked at review, removed after publication or reported by readers if it is misleading, repetitive or disappointing. KDP's other rules still apply too: you must hold the rights to everything you publish, your metadata must describe the book honestly, and you can't trade on other authors' names.

KDP's policies change, and this article summarises them rather than quoting them word for word. Before you publish, open KDP Help, find the Content Guidelines page and read the artificial intelligence section in full. Note the date you checked it.
bullets: Allowed: AI-generated text, images and translations, as long as you disclose them.
Required: an honest answer to KDP's AI question for every new or republished title.
Not a safeguard: disclosure won't protect a low-quality or misleading book.
Check first: the Content Guidelines in KDP Help (menu names may change).

sections.heading: AI-Generated vs AI-Assisted: Where KDP Draws the Line
paragraphs: KDP draws the line by asking who created the content. If an AI tool created the actual text, images or translation, KDP calls it AI-generated and you must disclose it. If you created the content and used AI only to edit, refine, error-check or otherwise improve it, KDP calls it AI-assisted and you don't have to disclose it.

Under KDP's guidance, brainstorming with AI also counts as AI-assisted, as long as you create the final text or images yourself. If you ask a chatbot for twenty possible chapter titles and then write the book yourself, that is generally AI-assisted.

The detail authors most often miss is that KDP still counts content as AI-generated even if you edited it substantially afterwards. Rewriting a chatbot's draft line by line does not make it AI-assisted under that definition. If you're genuinely unsure which side of the line you're on, the cautious choice is to disclose. You can also ask KDP support.
The scenarios below show how common uses of AI in a book generally fit KDP's published definitions.
bullets: AI-written chapters: ChatGPT, Claude or a similar tool drafted the text and you edited it. That's AI-generated text, so disclose it.
AI cover art: the image came from Midjourney, DALL·E or another image generator. That's an AI-generated image, so disclose it even if every word inside the book is yours.
AI editing only: you wrote the manuscript and used a grammar checker or chatbot to fix errors and tighten sentences. That's AI-assisted, and current guidance doesn't require disclosure.
AI brainstorming: AI suggested angles or an outline and you wrote everything. That's AI-assisted.
AI translation: you ran your own book through an AI translator to publish a Spanish edition. KDP lists translations as AI-generated content, so disclose it.
Mixed books: if only part of the book is AI-generated, such as the cover or a few illustrations, disclose those parts.

sections.heading: How to Answer KDP's AI Disclosure Question Accurately
paragraphs: The easiest way to answer KDP's AI question accurately is to keep a simple AI log for each book as you work, then copy your answers from it when you set up the title.

KDP asks the AI question as part of title setup, but its exact location and wording may change. If you answer yes, KDP may ask about text, images and translations separately, how much of each is AI-generated, how heavily you edited it and which tools you used. Read each option carefully rather than relying on screenshots in older tutorials.

A useful AI log has one row for each part of the book, such as the manuscript chapters, cover, interior images and any translation. A spreadsheet or notes app works fine. Use the columns listed below.
Your disclosure applies to the version of the book you publish. If you later swap in an AI-generated cover, add AI illustrations or publish an AI translation, update your answer when you republish.

If you hire a cover designer, illustrator, translator or ghostwriter, ask them in writing whether they used AI tools and for what. You are the publisher, so the disclosure is your responsibility even when someone else made the content.
bullets: Element: for example, 'Chapter 3 text', 'front cover image' or 'Spanish edition'.
Created by: you, a named AI tool, or another person such as a hired illustrator.
AI role: none, editing or proofreading, brainstorming, or generating the content.
Extent: none, some sections or the whole element, and whether you edited lightly or heavily.
Date and version: so you can tell what changed when you republish.
KDP category: AI-generated or AI-assisted, based on the definitions above.

sections.heading: Copyright Limits on Purely AI-Made Books
paragraphs: In the United States, text or images generated entirely by AI, without meaningful human creative control, generally can't be protected by copyright, because U.S. copyright law requires human authorship.

The U.S. Copyright Office issued registration guidance on works containing AI-generated material in 2023 and published a report on copyrightability in 2025. Broadly, it says copyright can cover your own writing, your creative selection and arrangement of material, and meaningful changes you make, but not the AI-generated parts on their own. When you register a work, you're expected to identify any AI-generated material in it. Federal courts have also upheld the human-authorship requirement, including in Thaler v. Perlmutter.

For a KDP author, weak copyright limits your control over the book, not your right to sell it. You don't need copyright to earn royalties. But if a competitor copies large chunks of raw AI text or reuses your AI-generated cover image, you may have little legal ground to stop them.

Copyright rules differ by country. The UK, for example, has a long-standing provision for 'computer-generated works', but how it applies to modern AI tools is debated and the government has been reviewing it. This is general information, not legal advice. If a book matters to you commercially, consult an intellectual property lawyer where you live.

The risk also runs the other way. AI output can closely resemble existing copyrighted text, characters or art, or include someone's trademark. KDP requires you to hold the rights to what you publish, and that responsibility is yours, not the AI tool's.
bullets: Generally protectable: your own writing, research, interviews, original photos and illustrations.
Potentially protectable: your creative selection and arrangement of AI material.
Generally not protectable in the U.S.: raw AI text or images you didn't meaningfully shape.
Check your AI tool's terms of service to confirm you can use its output commercially.

sections.heading: Why AI Books Get Rejected or Removed from KDP
paragraphs: KDP can block, reject or remove any book that breaks its content guidelines. Books heavy on AI content most often get into trouble for disappointing quality, duplicated content and misleading metadata.

KDP's guidelines describe content it may refuse because it gives customers a poor experience. Examples include books that don't deliver what the title and description promise, books barely different from others already in the store, and content that's freely available online unless you own the rights. AI tools make books like these quick to produce, which is why quality is the main risk for anyone publishing with AI.
The most common triggers for AI-heavy books are listed below, and a careful human review can catch each one before you publish.

Penalties can escalate. KDP may block a title before it goes live or remove it after customer complaints, and serious or repeated violations can put the whole account at risk of suspension or termination. KDP's terms and content guidelines set out the current enforcement details.
Amazon also limits volume. In 2023 it introduced a cap on how many new titles an account can create per day, widely reported at the time as three. Check KDP Help for the current limit.
Getting through review doesn't guarantee success. Readers who feel misled by AI filler often say so in reviews, and a new title with early negative reviews can struggle to recover.
bullets: Repetitive, generic text that circles a point without saying anything specific.
Invented facts, fake quotes or citations to sources that don't exist.
Titles, covers or author names that imitate a bestseller or another writer.
Titles and subtitles stuffed with keywords.
Near-identical books from one account, such as the same text with a new cover.
Public-domain or web content repackaged without meaningful additions.
Unchecked advice on health, foraging, safety, legal or money topics, where errors can harm readers.

sections.heading: Low-Content and Coloring Books: The Most Crowded AI Niches
paragraphs: Low-content books (journals, planners, logbooks and notebooks) and coloring books are among the most crowded categories on KDP, because templates and AI image tools make them quick to produce. Being allowed to publish there is not the same as being likely to sell.

KDP has a low-content option for paperbacks whose interiors are mostly blank or repeated pages. These books have different requirements from standard titles. For example, KDP doesn't require an ISBN for them, and some distribution options may not be available. Check KDP Help for the current eligibility rules before you choose this option.

You can judge how crowded a niche is without sales data. Search Amazon for the exact phrase a buyer would type, such as 'mandala coloring book for adults' or 'gratitude journal', look through the first few pages of results and watch for the warning signs listed below.

AI coloring pages have their own print problems: broken or unclosed lines, extra fingers, muddy grey shading, details too small to color, and images with too low a resolution for print. KDP's paperback guidelines recommend images of at least 300 DPI. Confirm the current requirement and order a proof copy before you publish.

To stand out in these categories, a book needs something AI can't supply. That could be real expertise (a climbing logbook designed by a climber), a narrow audience you understand well, hand-finished artwork, or prompts and instructions that are genuinely useful.
bullets: Dozens of covers in the same AI art style.
Near-identical titles and subtitles stuffed with keywords.
Top results with years of reviews behind them, which makes them hard to displace.
Reviews complaining about distorted images, repeated pages or ink showing through the paper.

sections.heading: The Money Side: Costs, Royalties and Taxes
paragraphs: KDP doesn't charge an upfront fee to publish, but a book made with AI can still lose money once you pay for AI subscriptions, editing, cover design, proof copies and advertising. No one can promise you any level of sales.

KDP royalties depend on the format, list price and marketplace, and on delivery costs for eBooks and printing costs for paperbacks. Royalty options change over time, so before you set a price, read the royalty and pricing pages in KDP Help and check the royalty estimates shown during pricing setup.

Treat your first book as an experiment and budget only what you can afford to lose. Many books sell few copies whether or not AI was involved, and paid ads can easily cost more than they earn if your book's page doesn't persuade people to buy.

Royalty income is generally taxable, and the rules differ by country. KDP's tax interview collects information for withholding and reporting, but it doesn't tell you what you owe where you live. Keep records of income and expenses, and check with your local tax authority or a licensed tax professional. This is general information, not financial or tax advice.
bullets: AI tool subscriptions (text and image)
Human editing or proofreading
Cover design or design software
Proof and author copies for paperbacks
Advertising, if you choose to run it
Your own time, which is the biggest cost for most authors

sections.heading: Who This Approach Is Not For
paragraphs: This guide is not for anyone hoping to mass-publish dozens of AI books quickly. That plan runs into KDP's daily title limit, its rules on duplicate and disappointing content, and categories already full of similar books.

The 'publish fifty books and let volume do the work' approach is widely promoted online, but its weaknesses multiply at scale. More books mean more skipped fact-checks, more chances of being flagged for duplicate content, more risk to your account and more negative reviews tied to your name.
The approach in this guide suits people willing to spend real time on fewer books. They use AI to speed up drafting and editing and keep their own expertise at the centre of the book.
bullets: Good fit: a subject-matter expert who wants AI to speed up outlining and editing.
Good fit: a novelist who writes the story and uses AI for brainstorming and proofreading.
Good fit: a hobbyist making one well-designed journal for a niche they know well.
Not a fit: anyone looking for passive income with minimal effort.
Not a fit: anyone unwilling to fact-check, edit and disclose honestly.

recommendations.best_for: Authors who wrote their own manuscript and want help with grammar, clarity and tone. KDP describes this kind of editing as AI-assisted. Check current plans and features on Grammarly's site.
recommendations.not_for: People who want a tool to write the book for them. If you use its generative features to write new passages, that content may count as AI-generated and need disclosing. It also doesn't replace a human editor for structure or fact-checking.

recommendations.best_for: Keeping research, chapter outlines and fact-check notes in one place, along with an AI log for each book that records which tool created or edited each part. The log makes KDP's disclosure question easy to answer accurately.
recommendations.not_for: Formatting the final manuscript for Kindle or print. You'll still need a formatting tool such as Amazon's Kindle Create, and you should check output in Kindle Previewer.

recommendations.best_for: Authors running publishing as a small business who want to track royalties, AI subscriptions, editing and ad spend in one place for tax time. Confirm current pricing and regional availability on the vendor's site.
recommendations.not_for: Hobbyists with one or two books, for whom a simple spreadsheet may be enough. It's an accounting tool, not a tax adviser, so check your local rules with a professional.

faq.question: Does Amazon KDP allow AI-generated books?
faq.answer: Yes. KDP allows books that contain AI-generated text, images or translations, but you must disclose that content when you publish or republish a title. The book must still meet KDP's content guidelines, so low-quality, misleading or duplicate books can be rejected or removed.

faq.question: Can I use ChatGPT to write a book and sell it on Amazon?
faq.answer: Yes, but text that ChatGPT or another chatbot drafts counts as AI-generated under KDP's definitions, even if you edit it heavily, so you must disclose it. You're also responsible for its accuracy and originality, and purely AI-written text may not be protected by copyright in the U.S. Books that add your own expertise, examples and fact-checking hold up far better with readers and in review.

faq.question: Do I have to disclose AI if I only used it to edit or proofread my book?
faq.answer: Under KDP's current guidance, no. Using AI to edit, refine, error-check or improve content you created yourself counts as AI-assisted, and so does using it to brainstorm ideas. If the tool wrote new passages or made images for you, treat those parts as AI-generated and disclose them.

faq.question: Will Amazon show readers that my book is AI-generated?
faq.answer: When Amazon introduced the disclosure requirement in 2023, it said it was not displaying the information publicly at that time. That could change, so check KDP Help for the current position. Either way, readers can often spot generic AI writing and may mention it in reviews.

faq.question: Can I copyright a book written entirely by AI?
faq.answer: In the United States, text and images generated entirely by AI generally can't be copyrighted, because copyright requires a human author. Your own writing, and your creative selection and arrangement of material, may still be protected. Rules differ by country, so talk to an intellectual property lawyer if this matters for your book.

faq.question: What happens if I don't disclose AI content on KDP?
faq.answer: Not disclosing AI-generated content breaks KDP's content guidelines. KDP can block or remove titles that break its rules, and serious or repeated violations can put an account at risk. Amazon hasn't published how it identifies undisclosed AI content, so the safest way to protect your account is to answer honestly every time.

conclusion: You can sell AI-generated books on Amazon KDP, but the rules reward honesty and quality, not speed. Disclose AI-generated text, images and translations, even if you've edited them heavily. Using AI only to edit or brainstorm counts as AI-assisted. Keep an AI log for each book so your answers stay accurate when you republish. Raw AI output gives you weak copyright protection, and crowded categories are unforgiving. If you're willing to put your own expertise at the centre and treat AI as a tool rather than the author, work through the 8-step checklist in this guide. Re-read KDP's current Content Guidelines before you click Publish, and treat your first book as a learning project rather than an income plan.
